import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.

noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,

noncomputable section

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/-

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/

/-

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/

end LeftHanded

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

section AltLeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

namespace AltLeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `AltLeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : AltLeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where

  invFun f := ⟨f⟩

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `AltLeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.

where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.

and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

noncomputable section

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,

noncomputable section

  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/

end LeftHandedModule

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

section AltLeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace AltLeftHandedModule

  left_inv _ := rfl

instance : AddCommGroup AltLeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `AltLeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence

instance : Module ℂ AltLeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `AltLeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : AltLeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where

  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

section AltLeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

instance : Module ℂ AltLeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : AltLeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

instance : Module ℂ AltLeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

instance : Module ℂ AltLeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `AltLeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : AltLeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where

  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl

noncomputable section

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/-!

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,

noncomputable section

  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

end LeftHanded

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,

noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.

noncomputable section

  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

section AltLeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

import HepLean.Lorentz.SL2C.Basic
/-!

## Modules associated with Fermions

Weyl fermions live in the vector space `ℂ^2`, defined here as `Fin 2 → ℂ`.
However if we simply define the Module of Weyl fermions as `Fin 2 → ℂ` we get casting problems,
where e.g. left-handed fermions can be cast to right-handed fermions etc.
To overcome this, for each type of Weyl fermion we define a structure that wraps `Fin 2 → ℂ`,
and these structures we define the instance of a module. This prevents casting between different
types of fermions.

-/

namespace Fermion
noncomputable section

section LeftHanded

/-- The module in which left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure LeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

namespace LeftHandedModule

/-- The equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
def toFin2ℂFun : LeftHandedModule ≃ (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun v := v.val
  invFun f := ⟨f⟩
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl

/-- The instance of `AddCommMonoid` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommMonoid LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommMonoid toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `AddCommGroup` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : AddCommGroup LeftHandedModule := Equiv.addCommGroup toFin2ℂFun

/-- The instance of `Module` on `LeftHandedModule` defined via its equivalence
  with `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
instance : Module ℂ LeftHandedModule := Equiv.module ℂ toFin2ℂFun

/-- The linear equivalence between `LeftHandedModule` and `(Fin 2 → ℂ)`. -/
@[simps!]
def toFin2ℂEquiv : LeftHandedModule ≃ₗ[ℂ] (Fin 2 → ℂ) where
  toFun := toFin2ℂFun
  map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
  map_smul' := fun _ _ => rfl
  invFun := toFin2ℂFun.symm
  left_inv := fun _ => rfl
  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

/-- The underlying element of `Fin 2 → ℂ` of a element in `LeftHandedModule` defined
  through the linear equivalence `toFin2ℂEquiv`. -/
abbrev toFin2ℂ (ψ : LeftHandedModule) := toFin2ℂEquiv ψ

end LeftHandedModule

end LeftHanded

section AltLeftHanded

/-- The module in which alt-left handed fermions live. This is equivalent to `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
structure AltLeftHandedModule where
  /-- The underlying value in `Fin 2 → ℂ`. -/
  val : Fin 2 → ℂ

/--

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
